item.title: Global Liquidity Peaks: The More Aggressively You Spent on AI in H1, the Sooner You Get Discounted
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-cn38ff4a-全球流动性见顶-上半年越激进砸-ai-的公司-越先被折价/
item.description: A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are now being discounted rather than rewarded.
item.content:encoded:
A stock market rally needs new money to keep buying. Global liquidity is already showing signs of peaking, and the companies that most aggressively invested in AI in the first half are now being discounted rather than rewarded.

This episode puts US AI capex, Hong Kong IPO activity, and household balance sheets on the same funding chain, offering a macro framework that does not treat AI as a cure-all.

0:33 Low IPO break rate is not a good sign
Do not take the low break rate of Hong Kong IPOs as a sign of market strength. In the first half of this year, the break rate was only around 10-20%, far below the normal level of roughly half-and-half under a market-driven mechanism, meaning the participants were mainly short-term speculative arbitrage funds, not long-term investors. Recently, the supply of new listings has decreased, and some IPO-related funds have had problems, but the two newly listed companies still broke their issue price, showing that temporary supply-side controls have not solved the fundamental problem: Hong Kong also faces peaking liquidity.

12:07 The more aggressive the AI spending, the sooner the punishment
Market sentiment reversed within a quarter. Before Q1, the capital market rewarded aggression: the louder the AI capex talk, the higher the valuation. By the end of July, when half-year reports were released, any major internet company that had made aggressive capital expenditures in H1—especially those that had burned through free cash flow—was discounted, and even Google was not exempt. Q2 was the quarter of maximum FOMO across the supply chain; everyone rushed to spend before prices rose, and inventory still supported gross margins. By Q3, inventory is depleted and the impact of price increases returns, so the negative factors will appear together.

15:54 Nvidia is closer to Cisco in 2000
Nvidia's earnings look good, but its cash flow is changing. Before the dot-com bubble burst in 2000, Cisco launched a 'lease-to-own' program to help customers finance purchases, recognizing future revenue as sales upfront. Nvidia is now also pushing lease-to-own. In its earnings report, free cash flow fell by half quarter-over-quarter, and accounts receivable are far above historical levels—which is speculated to be partly related to the credit enhancement and payment structure from lease-to-own. So Nvidia may have reached a point where it needs more aggressive financial measures to maintain capital market expectations, similar to Cisco's situation back then.

33:21 Primary market money comes from bullets three years ago
The answer lies in the timing of fund raises. The money that will be deployed aggressively in AI and robotics from H2 2025 to H1 2026 mainly comes from funds raised at the market peak in 2020-2022. From 2023 to 2025, they barely invested, until they saw state capital placing bets during a period when no one dared to invest and making the most money—the stories of ChangXin and ChangCun, two large language models, and two major chip companies stimulated market-based funds. The mentality is: copy the homework of state capital. So this is not a rational long-term increment, but more like a delayed emotional release.

47:31 New property policy removes households from the financing chain
The key of recent property policy is not to rescue developers, but to detach households from the old financing cycle. In the past, buying off-plan housing meant households played the role of financing counterparties in the investment-driven chain: paying first, receiving the property later. The policy pushes the chain toward marketization, so buyers purchase completed homes and only assume the consumer role, with risk reset to developers and financing institutions. The policy was introduced when house prices were near the bottom, to first stabilize the denominator on the asset side and avoid panic from breaking the chain during a decline. Japan after the 1990s and the consolidation of China's coal and mining industries followed similar paths.

1:01:34 Slow bull is not a slogan but a chip structure
A slow bull is not achieved by shouting but by layering market chips by duration: at the bottom are low-valuation, high-dividend blue chips held by insurers as long-term money that rarely trades; above that are public funds and index funds, functioning close to a price stabilization role; China Securities Finance and Central Huijin adjust the index at a higher level; and at the top are retail investors, private funds, and active management money. New insurance regulations require liabilities and assets to match in duration, yield, and liquidity, effectively ensuring that long money invests long, medium money invests medium, and short money invests short—not allowing short-term household money to be invested in ten-year illiquid assets.

1:22:49 Crises grow with each bailout; at least one and a half bubbles
Since the dollar left gold in 1971, global central banks have become increasingly accustomed to directly intervening in crises by printing money, with each action faster than the last. The quantitative easing after 2008 was supposed to be cleared during the rate hike cycle, but it was interrupted by political intervention, and then COVID hit in 2020, so an even larger wave of money printing was layered on before the previous bubble had dissipated—today we have accumulated at least one and a half bubbles. Central bank governors have learned to print even more money immediately when a crisis emerges, and the endogenous result is that inflation, financial asset appreciation, and wealth inequality all intensify simultaneously. As long as the bubble is not allowed to clear, the world may experience some form of prolonged stagflation.

item.title: Central Banks Won't Kill the $100 Bill: It's a $2.5 Trillion Interest-Free Loan
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-oddlots-央行不愿废除百元美钞-那是一笔-2-5-万亿无息贷款/

item.description: Cash use is declining, yet the dollar in circulation is at a record high. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: this money is essentially a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, at the cost of enabling global money launderers.
item.content:encoded:
Cash use is declining, yet the dollar in circulation is at a record high. Central banks have an incentive to keep printing $100 bills: this money is essentially a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the U.S. government, at the cost of enabling global money launderers.

This episode breaks down money laundering from 'bank wire transfers' to watches, tractors, casino chips, and VAT loopholes, and explains why central banks are reluctant to abolish the $100 bill.

5:09 Money laundering scale hasn't changed in three decades
The most commonly cited estimate for money laundering is 2% to 5% of global GDP annually, which at today's roughly $100 trillion GDP would be $2 trillion to $5 trillion. This figure comes from a rough estimate by former IMF chief Michel Camdessus in the late 1990s, and no one has been able to provide a better answer since. Oliver reminds us that what should be more alarming is that this percentage hasn't changed in thirty years: decades of anti-money laundering efforts haven't shrunk the criminal economy, only barely kept it from growing faster than the overall economy.

9:10 Banks spend $200 billion a year on AML with near-zero effect
Banks complaining about the cost of KYC is not just whining. In 1970, the U.S. passed the Bank Secrecy Act, and in 1989 the FATF globalized anti-money laundering norms, forcing banks to hire compliance teams and install AI monitoring software. LexisNexis estimates global AML compliance costs about $200 billion a year—enough to end world hunger and provide clean water to everyone. But the system generates a massive number of suspicious activity reports each year, and launderers still stay ahead of regulators. The problem isn't that banks aren't trying; it's that the whole system is costly, has weak feedback, and almost no one is held accountable for results.

12:14 Trade-based laundering is an order of magnitude bigger than cash smuggling
Cash smuggling makes laundering within the banking system look small, but the bigger chunk doesn't involve money at all: value is hidden in goods. Mexico receives about $25 billion in cash annually, while U.S. exports of John Deere and Caterpillar machinery become the goods that drug cartels buy with that cash; European luxury goods flow to China, and from China drugs and other goods are imported, with triangular trade settled through misinvoicing. Global Financial Integrity estimates trade-based laundering at about $1 trillion a year. A million-dollar watch worn through customs is far easier than carrying a million in cash.

17:18 The Vancouver model: Chinese cash demand meets drug cash supply
China limits each person to $50,000 in foreign exchange per year, yet wealthy Chinese have huge spending needs abroad. The Vancouver model matches this demand with the supply of U.S. dollars from drug cartels: cash bags are handed to Chinese gamblers outside Canadian casinos, the money is lost at the tables, and the gamblers owe a debt. That debt is offset by RMB transactions in China and subsequent drug sales. Viewed alone, the gambling looks like a loss; across the whole chain, it's a triangular settlement that simultaneously repatriates drug money and moves Chinese capital out. The model has since expanded globally, with luxury goods, daily necessities, and drugs all serving as vehicles for moving value.

23:25 VAT loophole lets the same goods repeatedly extract 20%
The EU's zero-rated cross-border transactions were meant to avoid tax authorities auditing each other, but they became an ATM: goods entering the UK from Ireland don't incur VAT, and when sold to a related shell company, 20% is added; that shell company exports the goods back to Ireland and can claim a refund from the UK tax authority for the 20% that was never paid. This circular movement is why it's called carousel fraud. The UK largely suppressed it with multi-agency crackdowns, but fraudsters then moved to mainland Europe, where it now amounts to about €50 billion a year, spreading from Lithuania to Portugal. Criminal organizations have no upper limit on competition: the more they cooperate, the bigger they get.

27:27 No one uses cash, yet central banks print record amounts
In the digital payment era, cash transactions have fallen to about 9% in the UK and 13% in the U.S., so by common sense, paper currency supply should shrink. After Bank of England Governor Andrew Bailey articulated the banknote paradox in 2009, the phenomenon intensified: the value of UK banknotes in circulation has doubled, and the U.S. is close to $2.5 trillion. Central banks attribute this to 'store of value,' but that doesn't hold—surveys show the average American adult has only a few hundred dollars on hand, while per capita currency in circulation exceeds $7,000. The Fed estimates about 65% of U.S. banknotes are held abroad, but that just pushes the question across borders: no one knows who actually holds these notes.

32:31 The $100 bill is a $2.5 trillion interest-free loan to the government
Seigniorage shouldn't be understood simply as profit from printing money: a $100 bill costs 9 cents to produce, but it isn't 'sold' to you—you can redeem it for goods at face value at any time, so cash held by the public is essentially an interest-free loan. With nearly $2.5 trillion in circulation, the U.S. government gets interest-free funds equivalent to about 6% of its national debt; federal interest payments currently account for about 19% of the budget, and if that $2.5 trillion had to pay interest, it would add about another percentage point. That's why central banks are reluctant to discuss abolishing the bill.

47:51 AML incentives are inverted: more reports, fewer criminals prosecuted
Suspicious activity reports were meant to be real-time intelligence for law enforcement, but reality is the opposite: banks hire thousands of compliance officers to file reports, law enforcement lacks resources to read them, and most reports go into a black hole; banks can be fined billions for missing a report, but get no reward for doing it right. Side effects include debanking—many people, often Muslims, are cut off from financial institutions. The guests' solution isn't to hire more compliance officers but to generate fewer reports, actually read them, and genuinely prosecute financial criminals, raising the cost of laundering rather than drowning everyone in paperwork.

item.title: Russia Is Stuck in Ukraine but Still Has the Strength to Open a New Front Against NATO
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-hiddenforces-俄罗斯陷在乌克兰-仍有余力对北约开新战线/
item.description: Russian forces have not won in Ukraine, but the war of attrition has produced the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience; the guest argues that Russia is fully capable of launching a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.
item.content:encoded:
Russian forces have not won in Ukraine, but the war of attrition has produced the world's most advanced drone-infantry combat experience; the guest argues that Russia is fully capable of launching a limited probe against NATO, and the window is in the final phase of Trump's term.

The guest is the chief foreign correspondent of the Wall Street Journal, who was in Kyiv on the day of the 2022 invasion; his assessment of Russian capabilities and European fractures is far more concrete than that of TV commentators.

19:16 Trump's Abandonment Rhetoric, Putin May Take It Seriously
Everyone is speculating whether John Ratcliffe's secret visit to Russia was about negotiating terms. The guest's judgment is that the visit was more like relaying a message from Trump to Russia: don't take the TV remarks that "America doesn't care about Europe" literally—if Russia invades Lithuania, Estonia, or Finland, the U.S. will send troops. The reasoning is that Moscow is bogged down in a war of attrition in Ukraine and urgently needs to cut off European support for Kyiv; escalating to probe NATO is one option, and Trump's earlier statements like "Europe is a bunch of freeloaders" give Putin room for misreading, hence the need for a dedicated trip to spell out the red lines. To be clear: the guest does not have intelligence from that room; he is explaining why this account "makes complete sense," not confirming it.

21:27 Russian Military Not Exhausted, Can Still Open a Limited Front
Is Russia, having failed to take Ukraine by force, incapable of opening another front? The guest's answer is direct: it absolutely can fight a "limited front"—not tanks crossing Poland all the way to Paris, but making trouble in the Baltic direction, such as sealing the Suwalki Gap, that narrow land corridor. He says the Russian and Ukrainian armies are the only two forces in the world that have turned modern drone-infantry warfare into a daily routine. Stories of Ukrainian 20-person drone squads wiping out entire traditional battalions are widely told, but the Russian side has the same technology: 20 Russians could equally eliminate a NATO battalion that hasn't been trained against drones. The outside world thinks Russia is getting weaker as the war drags on, but it overlooks that Russia is also the side being tempered in this technological revolution.

22:31 NATO Might Not Even Save Lithuania, Poland Included
A war game simulating a Russian invasion of Lithuania led the guest to a very unsettling conclusion: even Poland did not send troops to save Lithuania, let alone other allies. The reason is not insufficient military strength, but that Russian forces advance too quickly, and with the shadow of nuclear deterrence, allies would hesitate over "whether to enter," creating a chain of inaction. The guest says Moscow has factored this into its options. He also reminds that this is different from before 2022—then, one could clearly see over a hundred thousand Russian troops massing on the German-Belarusian border; now there is no such physical preparation. Therefore, the most direct escalation may not be a conventional invasion, but more small, ambiguous, deniable attacks (first hitting warehouses or drones).

23:40 Russia Probes NATO's Limits with Drones
In the current phase without signs of a massed army, Russia still holds a set of low-cost, low-attribution options: launching a limited strike on a NATO warehouse near Poland or Romania, or using captured and modified Ukrainian drones to create incidents, then watching whether NATO splits and whether the U.S. steps in. The guest points out that such probing is already underway—an armed drone struck a Ukrainian aircraft parked at Leipzig Airport in Germany, and only a drone malfunction prevented casualties; Russia's risk-taking behavior is steadily rising, and the West has yet to give a serious response. The senior European officers he has spoken with all believe the most dangerous window is the next one to two years, roughly falling in the final phase of Trump's term—the Kremlin will want to act before the U.S. might let go.

27:53 Putin Wants Ukraine Disarmed, Not a Ceasefire
Would Putin accept a decent ceasefire agreement? The guest's view is that just looking at what is on the negotiating table makes it clear: Russia's demands have always included not just territory, but also setting a cap on the size of Ukraine's military, restricting the types of weapons, and cutting off Western military aid to Ukraine. In his words, it is to make Ukraine "lose its ability to defend itself"; not neutrality, but "castration," so that it cannot resist again in the next phase of war—a year, five years, or ten years later. Putin signed Minsk-1 and Minsk-2, and violated both. So the guest quotes a former Ukrainian foreign minister's summary: this war will end in only one of two outcomes—the end of Ukraine, or the end of the Russian imperial project. Waiting for the other side to change its mind is not an option.

31:08 Street Protests Can Decide the Fate of a Wartime Cabinet
Kyiv's recent personnel earthquake appears on the surface to be an anti-corruption storm, but the key mechanism lies elsewhere: wartime has frozen elections, and the president's legitimacy now rests on only one ballast stone—"street support." Zelensky initially fired Defense Minister Fedorov, who championed drone innovation, because he needed the support of Commander-in-Chief Syrskyi; after Fedorov was dismissed, Kyiv's elite took to the streets in protest, small in scale but enough to make the president reverse course—he removed Syrskyi, replaced him with a younger general more popular at the front, and appointed a defense minister with an intelligence background acceptable to all sides. Ukraine's independent anti-corruption agency can still investigate people in the president's innermost circle; Zelensky once tried to amend the law to bring the agency under his control, but within a week he backed down under street pressure. When elections are absent, the square becomes the election.

38:37 Resistance Comes from Memory, Not Heroism
To sum up Ukrainians' perseverance as patriotic heroism misses what truly drives them. The guest says that after Russian forces take a Ukrainian town, one of the first things they often do is use bulldozers to demolish monuments to the victims of the 1930s Holodomor—they want to erase a memory. Russian state television talks about how to "re-educate" Ukrainians, making them forget their language and culture and become Russians. Around World War II, the Soviet Union carried out systematic purges of Ukraine's cultural elite; the guest, as a child, never knew those writers existed because the collective memory had been wiped out. Today's Ukrainians are almost all descendants of survivors of that meat-grinder history, carrying trauma in their bodies; it is the fear of "never again" that makes them prefer to die on the battlefield than return to those days.

45:59 Half a Million Veterans Held the First Wave of Collapse
On the night of February 23, 2022, most Kyivites still did not believe there would be war; the guest remembers that his experience in Kabul and Baghdad taught him that "impossible" can flip overnight, but ordinary Ukrainians had no such reference. What truly kept the country from collapsing in the first days was the eight-year war in Donbas: that fighting was far from Kyiv, but it trained roughly 500,000 Ukrainians who had fought against Russian forces, and volunteer organizations evolved into a flexible, daring force. The psychological threshold had already been crossed in Donbas—"we know what they look like, we know how to fight." Because of this experience, Putin's expected quick collapse did not happen, and the West's expectations were also broadly wrong.

item.title: Why Your Preschooler Is Hitting, Biting, or Kicking (And What Helps)
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-07-parentmojo-孩子打咬踢不是坏行为-是在夺回身体自主权/
item.description: Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting, and kicking are often the only tools left to shout, "I have no say" — when adults control nearly every aspect of their body. Give back a little choice, and the behavior will decrease.
item.content:encoded:
Stop asking how to make the hitting stop. For a three- or four-year-old, hitting, biting, and kicking are often the only tools left to shout, "I have no say" — when adults control nearly every aspect of their body. Give back a little choice, and the behavior will decrease.

Most approaches repeat "no hitting" and add punishment, without touching the need behind the behavior. This episode treats aggression as a need signal, and demonstrates scripts and cases for negotiating with teachers.

4:21 Hitting is a cry that the body isn't yours
Preschool is often the first place where a child is controlled by an adult other than their parents in nearly every physical arrangement: where to sit, how to sit, when to speak and move. In the previous three years, they could largely decide when to run and when to go to the bathroom. Sitting on the carpet for 20 minutes without moving is a real deprivation of autonomy; and a three- or four-year-old lacks the language to assert "my body, my rules," so hitting and kicking become one of the few tools left. So when you get that call from the teacher, don't rush to scold "keep your hands to yourself." Instead ask: how much say did this child have over their own life before this, and what can you give back now?

6:42 Preschool readiness is really obedience training
Teachers often say that a high proportion of children at a certain preschool are "kindergarten-ready," but the core definition of that readiness is compliance: when the teacher says sit, you sit, even if you're in the middle of something, even if your body is overloaded. Parents worry that if the child doesn't comply now, they won't get into a good elementary school, college, or good life. But the price the child pays for this definition is learning to suppress the feeling of "what I need right now." Teachers aren't villains either; they themselves need competence, child safety, ease, and even a sense of power. Many entered education to repair their own childhood trauma, but only know power-over relationships. Seeing both sides creates room for negotiation.

9:24 We accommodate ourselves, but refuse it to our kids
If adults feel overloaded at a party, we arrive early, leave early, retreat to a quiet room, or even wear noise-canceling earplugs — we find this natural. But when it comes to children, except for routine things like extra time on tests, we immediately worry that "too much accommodation will spoil him, and he won't survive in the real world." The truth is that adults grant themselves far more accommodation than they allow their children. The original text offers a concrete image: a bigger, stronger adult picks you up without explanation and carries you from a quiet room back to the middle of a noisy party — if it happened to an adult, you'd immediately see it as a violation of bodily autonomy; when it happens to a child, we look away.

12:11 The fix is before the behavior, not in it
Repeating "no hitting" doesn't work because that's not the knowledge the child lacks. You need a different set of questions: what happened in the seconds before the bite? What else happened earlier that day? Is there a move or a new baby in the child's life? A sensory-overloaded child who gets pushed in line may lose control, so let them stand at the front, back, or outside the line. A child who has trouble transitioning needs a few minutes' warning. Analogy to adults: when your partner snaps at you at night over nothing, it's often not about the current remark but about the morning argument, lack of sleep, and a string of stressors. If at that moment the other person says "your attitude needs work," you'd explode too; yet we often only do the latter to children.

15:10 Talking to the teacher: don't blame, hear the 'no'
Telling the teacher "please change your approach" will almost certainly hit a wall. A safer opening is to set aside judgment and reconstruct the facts: not who's at fault, just what actually happened; and include family changes, which are context the teacher can't see. Once you've figured out whether the trigger is sensory or about autonomy, then empathize with the three things behind the teacher's behavior: competence, child safety, and the need for a breather. The request must land on a concrete, executable change, like "Can the child sit on a ball outside the circle?" If the teacher refuses, the key isn't the refusal but the "no" — what need is the teacher still protecting? Find a way that meets both needs.

16:07 A nap conflict resolved without winners or losers
Jen's daughter Carys, at age three, couldn't nap. The teacher required her to lie down; she was bored and frustrated — her need was to play. The teacher had two needs: state regulations required offering a nap, and nap time was also the teacher's break. The solution they found was to move her mat to a slightly separated corner, where she could play quietly with soft toys that didn't roll, while the teacher could see her through the window from the break room. The child kept her right to free play, the teacher kept the rule and the break, and Jen escaped the dilemma of tattletale calls. This segment shows that "negotiating by need" isn't empty talk: everyone gives a little, but everyone's core need is preserved.

17:53 All methods boil down to one question
Compress all the above methods into one sentence: stop asking "how do I make the hitting stop," and ask instead "what need is this behavior communicating?" Hitting, biting, and kicking are surface signals; the real message might be "I need sensory relief" or "I need some say over my body." Once the need is correctly named, a path to meet it can be designed; and it's almost always the adult who changes the environment, because changing how the adult shows up is easier than changing the child.

item.title: Thailand Floods Wreck the Hard Drive Industry: The Biggest Falls, the Runner-Up Takes the Crown
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-asianometry-泰国洪水重创硬盘业-最大的厂跌倒-老二捡了王座/
item.description: A Thai flood reshuffled the hard drive hierarchy: Western Digital's shipments fell 51% quarter-over-quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook to take the top spot.
item.content:encoded:
A Thai flood reshuffled the hard drive hierarchy: Western Digital's shipments fell 51% quarter-over-quarter, while Seagate fell only 8% and overtook to take the top spot.

The geographic concentration of manufacturing supply chains carries risks, and this flood provided a complete case study—industrial estate siting, zero inventory, and single-point bottlenecks all detonated at once.

6:13 Flood barriers gave hard drive factories a false sense of security
The industrial estates sit on a floodplain north of Bangkok, converted from rice paddies. To guard against floods, developers built ring dikes up to two meters high, secondary wave walls, pumps, and drainage systems; the estates quickly grew into small cities with housing and shops. But this engineering may have misled everyone. When the real flood season hit in 2011, seven industrial estates were inundated within two weeks. Research later suspected that it was precisely this seemingly complete infrastructure that created a false confidence—the belief that even if it rained, all would be well. In other words, what manufacturers bought was not safety but an illusion of risk.

8:24 Reservoir releases were not the culprit; local rainfall was
After the disaster, dam managers were blamed for releasing water too late, with criticism focusing on favoritism toward farmers and rice corruption allegations. But research does not support this attribution. A 2023 simulation ran 17 scenarios of release strategies for two dams and concluded that even with perfect foresight of subsequent rainfall, the flooded area could be reduced by at most 3.68%. A 2020 study examining hydrological station data along the Chao Phraya River found that in one low-lying disaster area, less than 30% of the floodwater came from the river, while 73.7% came from local rainfall. In other words, the water fell directly on the disaster zone; reservoir decisions cannot bear that blame.

9:25 Why Seagate, untouched by floods, also ground to a halt
Seagate's factory in Korat was largely unaffected, but production still stopped—because seven of its top ten suppliers were flooded. A typical case was Japan's Nidec, which makes spindle motors for hard drives; two of its plants were submerged and halted production. The hard drive supply chain is tightly interlocked: no matter how safe the final assembly line, if motors don't arrive, the whole line stops. Seagate quickly qualified new suppliers, modified designs to reduce complexity, and negotiated payment terms with suppliers, limiting its quarterly shipment decline to 8%. In the same year, Western Digital's core plant was flooded to a depth of 1.8 meters, and quarterly shipments fell 51%. The difference was not in the height of their buildings but in which company's supply chain could route around the break faster.

12:34 Zero inventory amplified the flood into a global shortage
Before the flood, the hard drive industry had just gone through a round of consolidation: Western Digital announced the acquisition of Hitachi's hard drive business in March 2011, and a month later Seagate announced the acquisition of Samsung, bringing supply and demand barely back into balance. Because there was no surplus inventory to draw down, the shock was multiplied. Tom Coughlin estimated that demand in Q4 2011 was about 180 million drives, but actual production was only 110 to 120 million. And the flood hit right at the Christmas shopping season. Retail prices immediately rose 20% to 40%; a 1TB drive at Taipei's Guanghua Digital Plaza went from NT$1,750 to over NT$3,000. Even Intel admitted in December that Q4 revenue would be about $1 billion lower than expected due to the hard drive shortage. A localized flood, amplified by zero inventory, became a global shortage.

15:41 Floodwaters receded, but hard drive prices stayed high for two years
The water receded, but the shortage did not end quickly. Hard drive availability returned to pre-flood levels only about nine months later; retail prices fell even more slowly—on Newegg, prices did not drop back to pre-flood levels until April 2013. Backblaze, using its own purchasing records, calculated that the cost per GB in September 2011 was $0.044, and it did not return to that level until September 2013. Why is it easier to raise prices than to lower them? The author offers several interpretations: the ecosystem recovered more slowly than expected, the 2011 acquisitions by the two giants added extra costs, tablets caused a permanent decline in PC hard drive demand, and a more cynical guess—after Seagate and Western Digital acquired second-tier rivals, only three major players remained, making prices easier to 'stabilize,' or, in his words, to cartelize. As for which is the truth, he does not conclude.

18:47 The flooded giant chose to stay and build more walls
Western Digital's post-disaster choice is telling: it did not evacuate but doubled down on defense. WD and the Bang Pa-in estate owner built an 11-kilometer flood wall around the estate, and WD added a 6-meter inner wall around its factory; to add redundancy to its supply chain, in December 2011 it announced a new slider fab in Malaysia. A survey of 50 directly affected Japanese companies showed that nearly 80% decided to stay in Thailand. The reason is not hard to understand: existing estates, supporting infrastructure, and skilled workers are not easy to pack up and move. Thailand has since faced more major floods, especially in the 2020s, with almost annual occurrences; in November of the most recent year, it even rained what was called a 'once-in-300-years' event, but these estates have held so far. Whether stronger defenses will be needed in the future can only be tested by the next big flood.

item.title: AI Designs Viruses That Infect Bacteria, but Success Rate Is Only 5%
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-twiv-ai-设计出能感染细菌的病毒-但成功率仅-5/
item.description: AI has, for the first time, designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; the experimental validation success rate is only about 5%, far from the all-capable image portrayed in the media.
item.content:encoded:
AI has, for the first time, designed complete viral genomes from scratch that can infect bacteria; the experimental validation success rate is only about 5%, far from the all-capable image portrayed in the media.

This episode breaks down the success rate, compensatory mutations, and biosecurity rhetoric of AI-designed viruses, while demonstrating how observational vaccine studies can be refuted by E-values.

12:43 Vaccine switch as a natural control
The pitfall of the 'healthy vaccinee bias' is that vaccinated individuals tend to be more health-conscious than the unvaccinated, so comparing the two groups can mistake lifestyle differences for vaccine effects. This study exploits the 2017 US switch of the shingles vaccine from Zostavax to Shingrix: those vaccinated before the policy change received the old vaccine, and those after received the new one. Both groups are actively vaccinated, theoretically eliminating the bias. However, it is still not a randomized trial; unmeasured factors such as socioeconomic status, smoking, and diet may still be unbalanced between the two groups, so it can only be considered a quasi-experiment.

15:47 Weak confounding can overturn vaccine benefit
How strong must unmeasured confounding be to overturn an observational conclusion? The E-value measures this. This vaccine study has an E-value of only 1.42, barely above 1, meaning a confounder that is not particularly strong and is associated with both 'which vaccine received' and 'cardiovascular outcome' could explain away the observed risk reduction. An E-value of 3.4 or even 5 would indicate a robust conclusion; 1.42 is far from robust. The authors themselves admit that confirmation requires randomized clinical trials, and this observation should not be taken as evidence.

38:13 AI designs first functional viral genome
The researchers used the genomic language models EVO1 and EVO2 to write phage genomes: first training the models on vast amounts of public DNA sequences, then fine-tuning on PhiX174 to generate thousands of candidate sequences. When tested back in the lab, only about 5% of the products could actually infect E. coli. This is the first time AI has designed a complete genome from scratch that is proven functional. Media summaries that say 'AI directly creates viruses' miss a key point: the model has only seen sequences, with no experimental annotations telling it which base controls what function. The 5% hit rate shows how ignorant it still is about how sequence determines function.

44:37 Replication origin is the model's most conserved memory
Providing the model with just the first 4 to 9 nucleotides of the PhiX174 genome as a prompt significantly increases the accuracy of the generated results. The authors found that this unassuming sequence is part of the replication origin and is 100% conserved across all genomes generated by the model. It acts like a password saying 'I am a true virus': the model locks the replication origin as a core element, while allowing other positions to evolve freely. This also explains why such a short prompt is effective—the key is not prompt length but whether the prompt hits a functional Achilles' heel.

56:55 AI swaps one gene and adds 58 mutations itself
EVO36's design is not a full rewrite but a gene swap: replacing PhiX174's J gene with the shorter J protein from phage G4. When humans manually performed the same transplant in the past, the product could not infect; but EVO36, given by AI, infects normally because it has accumulated an additional 58 mutations across the genome. These mutations appear to be compensatory, allowing the foreign J protein to re-adapt to the local environment. Humans might not think to change 58 positions simultaneously; this is where generative models surpass single-point editing.

1:00:15 Phage cocktail defeats resistant bacteria
Natural PhiX174 hits a wall against already resistant bacteria, failing to break through even after five passages; a mixture of 16 AI-synthesized phages infects the resistant strain within one or two passages. The resistance is not broken by a single phage but by several synthetic phages recombining during replication, accumulating new mutations, and collectively breaching the barrier. This result suggests that phage therapy should bet on cocktails of multiple synthetic phages rather than a single strain.

1:07:29 Don't frame AI-made viruses as an urgent threat
For the study generating PhiX174, a commentary used the word 'urgent' to describe its biosecurity implications. Vincent directly opposes this wording on the show: the authors have already demonstrated through reproducible experiments that such research can be done safely, so the real task is not to sound the alarm but to start building a safety framework. He also emphasizes that reconstructing viruses is not science fiction as long as the sequence is available, which is precisely why we need frameworks, not panic.

1:35:53 Not vaccinating is often just not knowing
When discussing the unvaccinated population, the article raises an often-overlooked mechanism: some people do not get vaccinated not out of religious or ideological opposition, but simply because they do not know they should. Treating all vaccine hesitancy as a 'belief issue' misdirects policy—for these people, the key is not debate or persuasion but information outreach so they first learn the vaccine exists.

item.content:encoded:
Sports betting is becoming part of Gen Z's financial strategy, and its slow losses are harder to recover from than a single big loss. With betting and financial products on the same platforms, regulatory risk is widely underestimated.

From wealth management and market structure to regulation, this episode dissects the dangers of a gamified financial system, offering forward-looking insight into young investors' behavior and potential policy shifts.

3:06 Gen Z treats betting as a financial strategy
A Betterment survey found 26% of Gen Z investors view sports betting as part of a long-term financial strategy; a CNBC survey found 52% of Gen Z investors moved money from investments to sports betting in the past year. These figures match Dave's experience with young clients: betting has permeated every level of Gen Z, making it an issue wealth management must confront.

11:09 Slow losses are harder to recover from than a big loss
The insidious nature of sports betting is that it rarely produces dramatic big losses, but rather sustained small ones—like betting on hundreds of baseball games over a summer, losing 10% slowly each week, with the occasional 20% win that feels good, and the cycle repeats. This grinding financial despair is harder to recover from than a single big mistake; it's like a chronic tax on financial literacy.

17:14 Regulatory risk is widely underestimated
Dave argues that regulatory risk is overlooked by most because people assume regulation responds to catastrophic events, but it's more likely that a future administration or state regulator suddenly says 'enough.' He cites Florida and Texas being the first to ban speed cameras as an example of how regulatory moves are hard to predict. Thus, businesses relying on the current regulatory environment should be wary.

21:14 Leveraged ETF products raise market structure concerns
In the same week, South Korea imposed strict investor education thresholds for 2x leveraged products, Japan explicitly rejected single-stock leverage, while the U.S. saw applications for 2x leveraged products that reset hourly. Dave is more concerned that new ETFs try to hedge gambling risk with futures markets, but those futures markets don't exist until the ETF has assets—reversing the order, and potentially diverting resources from important financial participants who stabilize oil prices.

25:20 Tech giants' earnings show 'financial gimmicks'
Cameron points out that Nvidia extended accounts receivable to help customers, while hyperscaler customers extended accounts payable to beautify free cash flow; Microsoft reclassified some capital expenditures as investing cash flow to lower capex guidance; and activity in SPVs doesn't appear on the balance sheet. These 'financial gimmicks' are common at cyclical peaks; if fundamentals were strong, such moves wouldn't be necessary.

29:24 Reduced disclosure worsens information asymmetry
Cameron opposes moving to semi-annual reports with less disclosure, arguing it would worsen information asymmetry, benefiting institutions with resources to gather information via the 'mosaic effect,' and reducing market efficiency. He also notes that regulatory trends, like overturning the Chevron doctrine, concentrate power at the top, harming innovation and competition.

38:27 Cultural appropriation vs. adoption has a boundary
Cameron criticizes Urban Outfitters for selling Nirvana tie-dye sweatpants to 12-year-olds, seeing it as lacking respect for the context, but Dave argues it could be a gateway to the music—even if a kid initially likes just the smiley face, they might go on to listen to 'Heart-Shaped Box.' The debate reflects the tension between 'gatekeeping' and 'openness' in cultural transmission.

47:35 Finding role models as an adult means accepting imperfection
Dave shares how Keith Morris defused a conflict at a Circle Jerks show, sparking a discussion about role models. Cameron notes that as people age, they learn to appreciate others' strengths while accepting their flaws, just as they do with parents—taking the good and leaving the bad. Dave admits he can't find living role models because he knows no one is perfect.

item.title: Ion Drives: The Slow Rockets That Win Space
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-isaacarthur-离子推进-慢慢推-反而赢下太空竞速/
item.description: Rockets don't have to be more powerful to be better. Ion engines produce thrust as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet they can fire continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't match with minimal propellant—making them the workhorses of space logistics.
item.content:encoded:
Rockets don't have to be more powerful to be better. Ion engines produce thrust as gentle as a sheet of paper, yet they can fire continuously for years, accumulating speeds chemical rockets can't match with minimal propellant—making them the workhorses of space logistics.

This episode thoroughly explains the principles, limitations, and applications of ion propulsion, ideal for anyone wanting a systematic understanding of why electric propulsion dominates deep-space and satellite missions. If you're not obsessed with engine details, focus on the thrust and application segments.

1:04 Ion propulsion wins on endurance
The rocket equation is unforgiving: to go faster you must eject more mass or eject it faster, but carrying more propellant makes the vehicle heavier, trapping you in a tax-collector's loop. Chemical rockets use high thrust to escape Earth quickly, but their exhaust velocity is capped by the energy of chemical bonds. Ion propulsion takes a different approach: instead of burning fuel, it uses electric fields to accelerate small amounts of charged particles to extremely high speeds. The thrust is astonishingly low, but it can fire for weeks, months, or even years, eventually accumulating a delta-V that chemical rockets can hardly match.

4:04 Specific impulse and thrust are a trade-off
Specific impulse measures propellant efficiency: chemical rockets achieve only a few hundred seconds, while ion engines can reach thousands of seconds. But this high efficiency comes at the cost of very low thrust: ion engines can never lift off from Earth, the Moon, or Mars—at most, they could depart from a small asteroid where an astronaut could jump into space. It's not physically impossible; it's trading thrust for efficiency, trading time for speed. Chemical rockets are sprinters; ion engines are marathoners.

6:07 Two mainstream electric propulsion types
Classic gridded ion thrusters ionize propellant atoms and accelerate them through charged grids, offering high efficiency but suffering from continuous grid erosion. Hall thrusters use electromagnetic fields to ionize and accelerate propellant; they have lower specific impulse but higher thrust, making them the workhorses of modern satellites. There are also tiny electrospray systems for small satellites and high-power plasma concepts—the core differences all come down to how to generate enough electricity.

10:13 Why xenon is the default propellant
Propellant choice isn't intuitive: at the same acceleration voltage, helium ions fly fastest and xenon slowest, but thrust depends on momentum—mass times velocity—so helium looks tempting. However, at the same power, higher exhaust velocity actually means lower thrust; helium requires about 590 megajoules to ionize a kilogram, while xenon needs only about 9 megajoules. Xenon is an inert gas that doesn't corrode engines. It's today's premium choice for ion propulsion, but it costs around $1,000 per kilogram. Argon is much cheaper and is the industrial choice of the future.

18:20 Slow rockets are the backbone of space logistics
Ion propulsion is especially suited for missions after reaching orbit: spiraling up or down, rendezvousing with low-gravity small bodies. Humans are impatient cargo, but water, metals, parts, propellant, and other supplies don't mind slow transport. Future Mars missions or lunar bases might use chemical or nuclear thermal propulsion to move people quickly, while ion engines send cargo ahead slowly. Machines do the tedious work; civilization's history is written by carts, ships, trains, trucks, and containers.

26:25 Longevity is the core challenge, not a bonus
Ion thrusters must operate continuously for thousands or even tens of thousands of hours; grids erode, cathodes fail, and power processing units must survive years of operation. Chemical engines burn for minutes; ion engines burn for years—this isn't easier, it's harder in a different way. Additionally, they struggle to exploit the Oberth effect: chemical rockets can burn briefly and violently at periapsis to gain huge orbital energy, while ion thrusters spread their thrust over months, wasting that advantage.

30:26 Propellant is money, not just fuel
Propellant isn't just fuel; it's mass that must be launched, mined, processed, stored, transferred, and protected. Every kilogram of propellant saved means more room for instruments, shielding, cargo, and lifespan. The early space age was about getting to space; the next era is about moving cheaply in space. Ion propulsion may not put humans on Mars, but it could be the key tool for building space infrastructure—exploration gets headlines, logistics builds civilization.

31:26 Slow engines can build an interstellar civilization
Today's ion engines can't perform interstellar flights within a human lifetime, but far-future electric propulsion—with megavolt or even gigavolt accelerators, massive power systems, and propellant measured in tons—will begin to approach interstellar precursor vehicles. More critically, even if ion engines never become interstellar engines, they remain key to building the infrastructure of an interstellar civilization: before launching interstellar ships, you need to build collectors, mines, fuel depots, telescope arrays, habitats, and shipyards. These must be moved, assembled, maintained, and supplied, and ion propulsion may be the best option for these slow tasks. It's not the engine of interstellar ships; it's one of the engines that builds civilization, and then builds the interstellar ships.

item.title: Companies are becoming a series of loops | Anish Acharya (a16z)
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-06-lennys-公司变成一串自动循环-ai-能到坡顶-换山还得靠人/
item.description: Companies are being reshaped into a cascade of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, choosing the next mountain still requires human intuition.
item.content:encoded:
Companies are being reshaped into a cascade of interlocking loops; loops can push the current business to a local maximum, but after the plateau, choosing the next mountain still requires human intuition.

A structural take from an a16z partner: companies will be rewritten as loops, and the biggest consumer AI opportunity lies in joy, not efficiency. The views are often counterintuitive, useful for stress-testing your own product roadmap.

4:05 The AI era won't replicate winner-take-all
The AI era won't be winner-take-all the way mobile internet was: network effects once pushed search and social toward one or two players, but each layer of the AI stack now has about 20 relevant participants. Two years ago, everyone thought programming agents would end with a single winner; today Claude Code, Codex, Lovable, and Replit are all advancing simultaneously. Anish says the most cutting-edge people in the labs believe what's actually happening is autocatalytic effects—using new technology to improve your own processes—rather than recursive self-improvement, so there won't be a runaway winner that swallows everyone. The lesson for founders: don't bet everything on one full-stack giant; each layer (models, agents, interfaces) still has a long-term position.

10:08 CEOs want bigger companies, not fewer employees
Employees probably don't need to worry excessively about being replaced by AI, not because the technology isn't strong enough, but because CEOs are incentivized by growth, not shrinkage. Sundar doesn't want to run a more efficient $4 trillion company; he wants to build a $40 trillion one. A Google executive friend told Anish that the company hasn't laid off staff; instead, it used AI to compress a two-year roadmap into three months, and now the challenge is 'what to add to the roadmap.' When execution is no longer scarce, attention shifts from saving labor to finding new things to do for bigger goals.

15:12 Companies become loops; the next step needs humans
The corporate form is shifting from a list of roles and departments to a cascade of loops: starting with automation of individual workflows, then functional loops, then crossing business units, and eventually loops running most of the company's operations. Loops continuously produce outputs that become inputs for the next layer, and some mechanism feeds signals back to the CEO—when to adjust business entities, when to change strategy. This mechanism can help a company climb to a local maximum, but after reaching a plateau, it must rely on human intuition for out-of-distribution thinking to place the organization at the foot of the next mountain. Letting AI directly come up with an idea that can make a million dollars often fails, because humans can set the direction, while AI only sweeps along the established slope.

32:24 Users want to spend time, not save it
Silicon Valley's default is that AI's value is efficiency; Anish thinks this is a misjudgment: most people don't really want to save time, but to spend it on things that bring connection, love, progress, and fun. Historically, the biggest products have been entertainment and social, so the consumer AI opportunity is not 'saving a few more minutes' but creating loops that make people feel more connected, more loved, or experience progress or fun. He criticizes that technology over the past 40 years has extended intellect but hardly touched the soul; fitting AI into these desires is a product design challenge, not a model capability challenge.

37:29 AI is decoupling skills from desires
Anish believes AI is not just a productivity tool but more like an emotional and spiritual interface—it can separate 'skills' from 'desires.' People who want to make music are no longer blocked by 'not knowing how to play piano'; those who want to write programs don't need to first learn to a level where they could be employed; personal identity is thus amplified. He recalls that high-risk environments in the 1950s-60s greatly stimulated human potential, and believes the current world is in a low-risk state, where AI has the chance to lift GDP growth from 2% to 10-15%—provided it raises not the speed of individual steps but the scale of what groups dare to imagine.

1:04:42 Ideas too small now fail to raise funding
Investment criteria have reversed within three years. In the past, if a project was too ambitious, funds would often say a $100 million seed round was excessive; today at a16z, the reverse standard applies—if an idea, even with AI help, can only be that small, they simply don't invest. 'Unbounded ambition' has become the core value for screening companies; as Marc Andreessen puts it: we either go to the moon or leave a moon-sized crater.

1:09:48 Ship something small weekly to build product intuition
The most direct advice for product people is the old saying: build more. Pick a project you tell no one about, the smaller the better, treat it as a 'chassis,' run each new model through it, ship the result, and discuss it with people—this is the path to building AI intuition. The pace only needs to be one small release per week; being frantic is unsustainable. Anish himself used Codex to make a Mother's Day slideshow for his wife: pulling material from texts and photo albums, auto-scoring music, and finally generating 20 pages reviewing their relationship, even digging up old texts from their first date. The thing is small, but such works let you repeatedly taste AI's 'joy moments'—once tasted, your perspective never goes back.

item.title: American Outposts Were Danger Magnets: How the Counterinsurgency Trapped Itself
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-chinatalk-美军哨所是危险气泡-反恐战争如何困住自己/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-chinatalk-美军哨所是危险气泡-反恐战争如何困住自己/
item.description: American outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages but became magnets for violence. The more the military built, the heavier it got, losing mobility and eventually getting trapped by its own fortifications.
item.content:encoded:
American outposts in Afghanistan were meant to protect villages but became magnets for violence. The more the military built, the heavier it got, losing mobility and eventually getting trapped by its own fortifications.

Wesley Morgan witnessed the Afghan battlefield firsthand and spent a decade researching the deep contradictions of the counterinsurgency: tactical success alongside strategic failure. Anyone who cares about war and organizations should listen.

5:00 Outposts Were Danger Bubbles
In the summer of 2010, Wesley Morgan accompanied U.S. troops into the Pech Valley in Afghanistan and found that the outposts, meant to provide security for villages, actually became "danger bubbles" that drew conflict toward the villagers. U.S. forces and the enemy rarely suffered casualties; the real victims were the villages outside the outposts. This contrast made him ask: who built these outposts, why, and when? That led to his book The Hardest Place.

10:39 The Military Got Heavier and Heavier
From 2006 to 2010, U.S. forces in eastern Afghanistan gradually lost flexibility and mobility, tied to heavy outposts and MRAPs. In 2006, the 10th Mountain Division could still use pickup trucks and ATVs to reach remote areas, but by 2010, due to the IED threat and top-down force-protection requirements, conventional units could hardly get to those places, relying on special operations forces for offensive missions. This overextension meant follow-on units could not sustain the earlier operational reach.

12:51 Two ODA Teams: Restraint vs. Aggression
In 2004, two Green Beret ODA teams deployed to the Pech Valley in succession. The first, from the Utah National Guard's 19th Special Forces Group, used an "ink spot" tactic, trying to establish secure zones around district centers, and refused to enter the Korengal Valley because they sensed something there was luring them in. The second, from the 3rd Special Forces Group at Fort Bragg, was eager to enter Korengal to find a fight, but ended up embroiled in a local tribal timber dispute, used as enforcers for one faction, starting the Korengal "snowball" that grew into a years-long intense battlefield.

19:27 Three Tribes Inside the Military Were Incompatible
In eastern Afghanistan, there were three "tribes" within the U.S. military: conventional forces, Green Berets (who worked with local partners, training Afghan National Army commandos and local police), and the Joint Special Operations Task Force (like Task Force 373, mostly SEAL Team Six and Rangers, conducting night raids). These three had different goals, sometimes supporting each other but more often getting in each other's way. For example, a task force might kill someone who could have been easily arrested by conventional forces, and only the task force could reach remote areas that conventional forces couldn't. This lack of coordination was a core problem of the Afghan war.

24:56 Commanders Measured Success with Wrong Metrics
Many commanders lacked a real understanding of counterinsurgency and fell back on quantifiable performance metrics: tons of ordnance dropped, miles of roads built, number of meetings held. The book cites the 2nd Battalion, 503rd Infantry Regiment, which fought in Kunar Province for 15 months, losing 24 soldiers. Its commander, Lt. Col. Bill Ostland, defined success by the number of JDAMs dropped, ammunition expended, SERP budget spent, and 10,000 Beanie Babies distributed—metrics that didn't reflect actual effects and were even self-contradictory.

40:00 Naval Officers' Unusual Land-Warfare Credentials
Wesley Morgan points out that many current senior U.S. Navy and Air Force officers have a chapter in their careers that diverges from the conventional path: they led Provincial Reconstruction Teams (PRTs) in Kunar and Nuristan provinces, including submarine officers, nuclear engineers, and naval aviators. For example, the current commander of Indo-Pacific Command, Sam Paparo, led a PRT in Nuristan for a year. These missions happened alongside the fighting in Wana and Narisan; they went out daily in MRAPs on counterinsurgency missions. This experience became a distinctive mark on their careers.

43:18 Military-Media Relations Went from Transparent to Toxic
Morgan recalls that in 2007, as a 19-year-old freelance journalist, he could almost freely choose which units to embed with; public affairs officers just helped him get to company- and platoon-level units. But now, since the embed system ended in 2013-2014, the military's relationship with the media has deteriorated sharply, and a new generation of battalion- and below-level officers sees the media as something to fear. He believes the turning point was not the McChrystal incident but after Obama's second term, when the military began restricting embeds, keeping the war out of sight because the complicated message that "advisors" were really "combat advisors" was unwelcome.

57:52 How Multicam Became a Mark of Eliteness
Morgan tells the story of how Multicam camouflage spread: invented around 2002 by a Brooklyn art school graduate, it lost the Army's competition (the Army chose the ineffective ACU pattern), but Delta Force adopted it privately because ACU performed poorly at night. It then spread through special operations circles, becoming a mark of eliteness. The key was that Crye, the company, hinted to game developers that this was the elite camouflage, so Multicam appeared in games like Ghost Recon before real photos did, building an elite image in young soldiers' minds.

item.title: Kent State Shootings: Why the National Guard Fired on Students
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-05-extracredits-肯特州立枪击-国民警卫队为何向学生开火/

item.description: In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on student protesters, killing four. Confused orders, outdated tactics, and armed confrontation turned a peaceful protest into bloodshed.
item.content:encoded:
In 1970 at Kent State University, the National Guard opened fire on student protesters, killing four. Confused orders, outdated tactics, and armed confrontation turned a peaceful protest into bloodshed.

This episode reconstructs the full sequence of the Kent State shootings, revealing the chaos and misjudgment behind the events, and directly helps understand the social fractures of 1960s-70s America.

1:05 National Guard armed presence on campus
On May 3, 1970, 850 National Guardsmen with M1 rifles, bayonets, and tear gas arrived at Kent State University, bivouacking on the football field to guard the ROTC building. The deployment enraged students; even those not normally involved in protests felt the war had come to their doorstep. But students were not particularly afraid, because previously the Guard had handled demonstrations with tear gas or scuffles, never firing live ammunition. This time, however, the troops carried live rounds.

3:08 Confused orders, governor stoking the fire
Governor Rhodes's rhetoric was inflammatory, comparing protesters to Nazi Brownshirts and the KKK, calling them 'the worst people in America.' But in fact, his order to deploy the Guard was not official until May 5, while troops had arrived on May 3. There were serious disagreements among the university president, local government, and governor over the Guard's mission: the president believed the assembly had been banned, but protest leaders and professors pointed out the ban had not yet taken effect. This confused communication set the stage for the later conflict.

5:09 Last-minute rule change sparks standoff
On the evening of May 3, students gathered on the Commons to protest, but local authorities moved the curfew from 1 a.m. to 9 p.m. and sent police to disperse them. Students saw this as 'changing the rules mid-game' and split into two groups: one went to the president's house to demand First Amendment rights and was driven back with tear gas; the other sat down in the middle of a main road to block traffic, singing 'Give Peace a Chance.' Police and Guardsmen surrounded them, with helicopters overhead. Eventually, the Guard used tear gas and bayonets to push students back to the dorms, resulting in at least two students stabbed and 68 arrested.

9:11 May 4: peaceful rally resumes
On the morning of May 4, around 2,000 students gathered again on the Commons. Although no official state of emergency existed, university officials distributed flyers declaring the assembly illegal. Guard commander General Canterbury insisted the demonstration was unlawful, but students still spread word of the rally via loudspeakers. By noon, the rally was largely peaceful, aside from some vulgar chants. Campus police used a loudspeaker to declare the assembly illegal and order dispersal, but the voice was drowned out, and a few rocks were thrown at vehicles. Canterbury then ordered two volleys of tear gas, but they missed, and the wind blew the gas away.

12:13 13 seconds of fire, 67 bullets
The Guard advanced to clear the area, successfully dispersing most protesters, but a group of 52 advanced too far and were trapped against a fenced-in practice field, pelted with rocks. After 10 minutes, they received an order to withdraw toward Taylor Hall. When they reached the top of the hill, 72 Guardsmen turned, raised their weapons, and fired for 13 seconds, a total of 67 bullets. Four students died: Jeffrey Miller (20, 265 feet away), Allison Krause (19, 340 feet away), Sandra Scheuer (19, 390 feet away), and William Schroeder (19, 390 feet away). Nine others were wounded, from as close as 60 feet to as far as 750 feet.

14:16 A photograph changes America
After the shooting, there was a dead silence; students stood frozen. Fourteen-year-old Mary Ann Vecchio knelt over Jeffrey Miller's body screaming, and 21-year-old photography student John Filo captured the image that would shock the nation. But the conflict was not over; protests spread across the country, followed by the hard-hat riot and the Jackson State shootings. The program emphasizes that this history has striking parallels to the present and is worth reflecting on.

item.description: Olympe de Gouges is known for her Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but her death was not due to her feminist advocacy, but because she opposed the execution of the king and attacked Robespierre.
item.content:encoded:
Olympe de Gouges is known for her Declaration of the Rights of Woman, but her death was not due to her feminist advocacy, but because she opposed the execution of the king and attacked Robespierre.

To understand the political situation and personal fate of women during the French Revolution. History enthusiasts and those interested in feminist issues will find it compelling.

1:05 The Declaration of the Rights of Woman Responds to the Declaration of the Rights of Man
Olympe de Gouges is best known for her 1791 Declaration of the Rights of Woman and the Female Citizen, a direct response to the 1789 Declaration of the Rights of Man and of the Citizen. The original used citoyen; she changed it to the feminine form citoyenne, which looks quite different but sounds similar. Her writing and political activity went far beyond this pamphlet, and her execution was not due to her calls for women's rights.

6:13 Biographical Truth Is Mixed with Fictional Invention
The first English biography of de Gouges, Women's Rights in the French Revolution, heavily cites her epistolary novel Memoirs of Madame de Valmont as factual evidence, but this book is highly fictional. The protagonist is widely considered to be her own stand-in, while the Marquis de Flaucour represents her possible biological father, the Marquis de Pompignan. This lineage remains unconfirmed to this day.

14:19 The Comédie-Française Suppressed Female Playwrights
Zamore and Mirza was written in 1784 and submitted anonymously; it was accepted the following year but delayed in performance. After de Gouges repeatedly pressed the matter, the theater revoked her admission rights and sought her arrest. Between 1761 and 1789, the theater accepted only nine plays by women, and she was the only writer treated this way. She later wrote to the Duke of Richelieu, who helped restore her status.

17:28 The Slavery Play Became the First Abolitionist Drama
In 1789 the play was finally performed, but the setting was changed from the East Indies to the Caribbean, and the characters from Asians to Africans, with the title changed to The Slavery of Blacks. It is often considered the first French play explicitly supporting abolition and told from the perspective of the enslaved. Abolitionists praised it, while wealthy colonists hired hecklers to disrupt performances, and actors refused to darken their skin for the roles.

23:32 The Article Mirrors the Original 17 Articles One by One
The Declaration of the Rights of Man granted civil rights but excluded women, and the 1791 Constitution limited voting rights to taxpaying men. De Gouges's Declaration of the Rights of Woman copied the format of the 17 articles, rewriting each one. For example, where the original Article 10 guaranteed freedom of speech, she added that mothers had the right to publicly declare the father of their children. The entire document was dedicated to Marie Antoinette, encouraging her to advance women's rights.

28:39 Defending Louis XVI Became a Liability
Despite her revolutionary stance, de Gouges believed constitutional monarchy was best for France, and that the king should be a symbol rather than a power. During Louis XVI's treason trial in 1792, she voluntarily defended him, arguing that since the monarchy had been abolished, the Republic could not judge the king for actions taken while he was in office. Her logic was criticized as far-fetched; the king was ultimately executed, and she herself was seen as a royalist.

30:43 Federalist Advocacy Led to Her Arrest
In July 1793, de Gouges suggested that French provinces should govern themselves rather than be a unified republic, which was seen as a direct provocation. She underestimated the intense political atmosphere of the Reign of Terror, and voluntarily led investigators to her office, believing her works would prove her loyalty. Instead, her unfinished play France Preserved, which sympathized with Marie Antoinette, was used as evidence against her. She was ultimately executed on charges of opposing the republican constitution.

item.content:encoded:
Heart Aerospace's ES-30 electric aircraft takes off on $5 of electricity, with operating costs 48% lower than older models, targeting half of all flights under two hours and using hybrid power to solve backup battery challenges.

This episode traces the seven-year journey from a 3D-printed model to a 100-foot wingspan aircraft, revealing the economics and technical breakthroughs of electric aviation, and is highly inspiring for those interested in clean energy and transportation innovation.

0:00 Electric aircraft costs just $5 to take off
Heart Aerospace's ES-30, the world's largest electric aircraft, has successfully completed its first flight. With a 100-foot wingspan and a takeoff weight of 25,000 pounds, it costs only $5 in electricity to take off. Its all-electric range is 125 miles, extending to 500 miles with hybrid power, and charging takes about 30 minutes. This marks the viability of electric aviation in the regional market, with operating costs 48% lower than traditional aircraft.

1:30 Electric motors replace jet engines
Heart's aircraft replaces jet engines with electric motors, which have only one moving part, no combustion, and almost no wear, making them cheaper to produce and more reliable. In contrast, jet engines have thousands of parts and burn fuel at extremely high temperatures. Electric motors are nearly silent during taxiing and offer good torque characteristics, significantly reducing noise and vibration.

3:00 Regional aviation has been neglected by technology
The complexity of jet engines makes the cost of engines for 30-seat and 70-seat aircraft similar, leading airlines to favor larger planes and longer routes, making short regional flights highly inefficient. Half of all global flights are under two hours, but existing technology cannot effectively serve this market. Heart targets 40-year-old aircraft models; the key to regional connectivity is flight cost, not distance.

4:09 From a Swedish air force base to MIT
Anders grew up near a Swedish air force base, passionate about aircraft, and later pursued a PhD in jet engines at MIT. Twelve years ago, Elon Musk's MIT talk about electrifying all forms of transportation became his inspiration. He spent days researching jet engines and nights tinkering with drones, and with Swedish government funding, built relationships with Scandinavian Airlines, laying the groundwork for his startup.

6:00 YC startup: from LOI to physical prototype
At YC, Anders started with a 3D-printed model and letters of intent (LOIs) from airlines like SAS. They first built a 400-kilowatt motor, which attracted pre-orders from United Airlines, leading to more capital. Anders emphasizes that each funding round requires tangible progress, preferably a physical, touchable result, which is more convincing than a business plan.

7:00 United came from a spam email
Heart's first major customer, United Airlines, came from a spam folder. Clara discovered the inbound email while cleaning spam and invited them for a visit. After seeing the electric motor, United immediately understood and placed an order. This highlights the importance of showing physical products directly and how unconventional channels can bring huge opportunities.

8:00 In-house manufacturing and testing
Heart designs and builds most aircraft components in its Los Angeles factory, including actuators and fuselage. They choose to manufacture critical parts in-house to avoid dependence on single suppliers and accelerate iteration. The entire factory acts as a large test bench, where faults can be injected to ensure systems operate safely under abnormal conditions.

10:00 Battery and hybrid solution
Heart's battery lab tests cells from Chinese, American, and Korean manufacturers, with current highest energy density at 370 Wh/kg, approaching the 400 Wh/kg target. To solve backup battery issues, they employ a hybrid system using a simple turboprop engine as backup, adding about 20% upfront cost but enabling a 500-mile range and meeting safety reserve requirements.
